slides.title: Observe a queue
slides.keyIdea: A queue stores arrivals until a worker can serve them.
explanation: Imagine a desk receiving one card each minute. Each card waits until the desk is free. This original toy example explains the distinction between arrival and service.
The source picture contains three cards and one desk. Count only the cards waiting, not the card already being served.
Study question: if the worker serves two cards per minute and one new card arrives per minute, what happens to an existing backlog? State your assumptions before answering.
slides.caveat: Original synthetic demonstration. No course slides, transcript, or measured data are reproduced.

slides.title: Track the balance
slides.keyIdea: Next backlog = current backlog + arrivals − completed service.
explanation: Start with three waiting cards. Two new cards arrive, and the desk completes one card. The resulting backlog is four cards.
This is an accounting identity for the stated interval, not a prediction of random arrivals. Keep the counting boundary consistent.
Worked example: 3 + 2 − 1 = 4. If there is no backlog, completed service cannot exceed available work.

slides.title: Name the uncertainty
slides.keyIdea: A toy example does not establish a real service rate.
explanation: A diagram can illustrate a mechanism without providing measurement evidence. Do not treat illustrative quantities as observations.
No transcript or video is supplied in this demo. These notes are original supplemental explanations, not instructor speech.
Review question: which extra measurements would you need before estimating waiting time in a real queue?
